channel.title: Spite Frequencies
channel.description: Music made where it wasn't wanted, and songs that kept the score.

item.title: Kept by Accident
item.description:
Most music disappears. These recordings didn't, mostly by luck.

There's a Ghanaian rap tape pressed in about fifty copies and found years later in a market. A Gnawa master shares a cassette with a drummer nobody can name. Forty grimy tapes come out from behind a butcher's counter in Queens, and nine reporter's cassettes from a Cape Town cellar. From Vilnius come home tapes that existed in a single copy, and from Lithuania a whispering tape almost nobody heard. A Japanese label released exactly 222 cassettes of strangeness. And one stranger paid to turn her poem into a record.

If one of these is yours, tell us.

item.title: Say It Without Saying It
item.description:
A mixtape about what happens when someone in power decides a song is dangerous.

It opens in Cairo in 1919, where a fruit-seller's cry carried a banned man's name. Then come a samba that teased the police chief and a raï singer her own new state took off the air. Next, music bootlegged onto hospital X-rays, and a wartime cantata that survived only on tape. Two Baltic bands follow: one whose recordings the radio destroyed and the band itself kept, and one banned for a train its fans wrecked. It ends in London in 2019, with the first song a British court punished someone for performing.

Each time the music changes carrier, code or country. It does not go away.

item.title: “My name is Gauhar Jaan!”
item.description:
In November 1902 the Gramophone Company set up a makeshift studio in two hotel rooms in Calcutta. The singer who climbed up to the horn was Gauhar Jaan, a courtesan-artist at a time when reformers were trying to legislate her profession out of existence. She sang a khayal in Raag Jogiya, then shouted her own name at the end so no one could mistake whose voice it was.

She went on to record more than 600 songs in some ten languages. She was not supposed to be the voice of a nation's first record. She made herself impossible to forget.

item.title: Whispers, flutes and a tape almost no one heard
item.description:
Don Campau's Living Archive of underground cassettes has a short entry on Echidna Aukštyn, a Lithuanian ensemble led by Ramūnas Jaras. Their tape from around 1993 is a bizarre mix of creepy whispers, dark instrumental passages, free improvisation, echoing voices, field recordings and flutes.

Two tapes, a name, and a description. This is what most of the world's music looks like once it has slipped out of memory. If you made it, or own it, we would love to hear from you.

item.title: Thirty songs left in the radio archive
item.description:
In Soviet Estonia, the Estonian Radio studios were almost the only place a musician could record. Velly Joonas recorded about thirty songs there, and nearly all of them stayed in the archive.

One that escaped, decades later, is "Stopp, seisku aeg!" ("Stop! Stall the time!"). She wrote an Estonian lyric to a Frida song and sang it over an amateur band of young Russians from the Lasnamäe district. The Tallinn label Frotee put it out on a 7" in 2015, and has since dug more buried tracks out of the radio archive.

item.title: The teenage tape you hear on hold
item.description:
In 1989 Tim Carleton and Darrick Deel, both about sixteen, recorded a smooth little instrumental on a four-track in a garage. It ended up as the default hold music on Cisco phone systems, and so it has been played to millions of people who never chose to hear it, while they waited.

A home-made tune became the world's most unwanted repeat listen. Carleton says he never handed over the ownership.

item.title: The song that sang a banned name without saying it
item.description:
In 1919 the British exiled Saad Zaghloul, the leader of Egypt's independence movement. Egyptian accounts say the military authorities then made it an offence even to say his name, punishable by prison and the lash.

The answer came from the street-song writers Badīʿ Khayrī and Sayyid Darwīsh: a little ṭaqṭūqa apparently about dates. Zaghlūl is also a variety of date. "O Zaghloul dates, O sweet dates" is a fruit-seller's cry that a whole city could sing while meaning the man.

The voice on the record is Naʿīma al-Miṣriyya, Cairo's "queen of the records", a woman who made around 150 discs. When it was recorded is still argued over: one scholar files her first Mechian session under 1915, which cannot fit a tribute to a man exiled in 1919. Her personal archive is being digitised, and the answer may be in there.

item.title: The song a poll said nobody wants
item.description:
The artists Komar and Melamid and the composer Dave Soldier asked about 500 visitors to the Dia Center's website what they least wanted to hear in music. The answers included bagpipes, accordion, cowboy music, opera, rap, tuba, drum machines, advertising jingles and children's voices.

Then they put all of it into one 22-minute piece, with a children's choir urging you to shop at Walmart. It is a song engineered to be unbearable, and it is a lot of fun.

item.title: The only recording of the noise machines
item.description:
Luigi Russolo built intonarumori, "noise-intoners": boxes with cranks and levers that howled, crackled, gurgled and buzzed. His first concert with them, in Milan in 1914, ended in a riot.

The machines themselves are gone. Of everything he wrote for them, only a fragment of one score survives. What does survive is one gramophone disc made with his brother Antonio in 1921: "Corale" and "Serenata", where a fairly ordinary little orchestra is shadowed and interrupted by a roar nobody can quite place. The French national library lists it as Grammofono R6920, issued in 1924.

It is music aimed at an audience, from people who wanted a fight. The Futurists' later closeness to Mussolini belongs in the story too.

item.title: The grandmother of raï, banned from her own country's radio
item.description:
Cheikha Rimitti could not read or write. She learned her trade singing at weddings and in the bars of western Algeria. In 1954 her song "Charrak Gattà" ("Tear, lacerate") went straight at the taboo of virginity and scandalised the pious.

After independence in 1962, the new government denounced her songs as "folklore perverted by colonialism" and banned her from radio and TV. She kept singing at weddings, then in Paris, until two days before her death in 2006.

item.title: The first song a British court punished someone for performing
item.description:
In August 2018 the Metropolitan Police obtained a gang injunction that barred the drill duo Skengdo x AM from performing certain music. In December they performed their song "Attempted 1.0" at a concert in Camden. In January 2019 a court gave them nine months each, suspended for two years. It was widely called the first prison sentence in British history for performing a song.

The injunction was lifted in 2021. Whatever one thinks of the lyrics, it is a modern case of a state deciding a song is a weapon, like the ban on Zaghloul's name in 1919.

item.title: The band whose tapes the radio destroyed
item.description:
On 22 September 1980, the Estonian punk-art band Propeller played at half-time of a football match between Estonian Radio and Estonian TV staff at Kadriorg Stadium. Alarmed by the crowd, officials cancelled the second set. A riot followed and unrest spread through Tallinn. Forty intellectuals then wrote their famous open letter of protest.

The band was made to disband, singer Peeter Volkonski was banned from the stage, and Estonian Radio destroyed its Propeller recordings. But the band had kept its own copies, and in 1995 the 1980 tapes came out as their only album.

item.title: The ballad that convicted Robert Ford
item.description:
Robert Ford shot Jesse James in the back for the reward, was pardoned, and never escaped the song. "The dirty little coward that shot Mister Howard" was passed around as a public verdict the courts never delivered.

Bentley Ball recorded it for Columbia (A3085) in 1919, one of the earliest commercial versions. It is a folk court in waltz time, and Ford is still guilty in it.

item.title: The Workshop for the Restoration of Unfelt Feelings
item.description:
NSRD was a Riga collective of artists, Hardijs Lediņš and Juris Boiko at the core, who made a wonky, home-taped experimental pop that hardly anyone in the Latvian SSR wanted to hear. Albums like Invalīdu tramvajs ("Invalids' Tram", 1983) existed mostly on cassettes and reel-to-reel. Every year they walked the Bolderāja railway line as an art work.

A small archive label on the edge of Riga, Underbed Storage, now puts out their unreleased reels, along with tapes from the old DIY label T.U.M.S.A. Home Rec.

item.title: Settling a quarrel with a drum
item.description:
In East Greenland, two people with a real grievance could take it to the whole settlement. Each stood with the frame drum and sang mocking songs at the other. The audience laughed, and the laughter was the verdict. It was a grudge given rules, a stage and a judge, and no one had to die.

In 1906 the Danish linguist William Thalbitzer carried a phonograph to Ammassalik, now Tasiilaq. A woman he wrote down as K'iwingatāk' sang a duel song into the horn. It lasts about a minute.

The cylinder survives in Copenhagen and was published on Inuit: 55 Historical Recordings (ULO, Nuuk / Sub Rosa). These are Greenlandic cultural recordings, and any further use is for Greenlandic voices to decide.

item.title: Rough music: when a village plays you out of town
item.description:
Across Europe there was a custom with many names: charivari, cencerrada, scampanata, Katzenmusik, rough music. When a community judged that someone had broken its rules, it gathered at night outside their door and made the worst noise it could: cowbells, pans, horns, whistles. Often the target was a widow or widower who had remarried. The noise was the sentence.

A Spanish cencerrada was taped in Salamanca in 1984 and sits in the Fundación Joaquín Díaz archive. The same habit of banging pans returned as political protest in the 2011 caceroladas.

item.title: Nine cassettes from a Cape Town cellar
item.description:
In 1986 a 25-year-old radio reporter, Nigel Wrench, recorded South Africa in the most brutal years of late apartheid. His cassettes ended up in the archive of Turnstyle News, in a Cape Town cellar, and stayed there for decades.

Edited from nine of those tapes, ZA86 came out on the 25th anniversary of Mandela's release. Among the street sound and interviews is a Band Aid-style pop song released by the apartheid regime itself, the state trying to sing its own way out.

item.title: Music on the ribs
item.description:
After the war, huge amounts of music were forbidden in the Soviet Union: jazz, rock'n'roll, émigré singers, tango, prison songs. Bootleggers worked out that discarded hospital X-ray film could take a groove. Cut into a rough disc with a cigarette-burned hole, someone's chest or skull became a record of Elvis or a banned émigré crooner.

They were called "ribs" or "bones". The state switched the medium off by banning the music; the music simply moved onto the X-rays.

item.title: Mary Bolton's song
item.description:
For most of the twentieth century, magazines carried small ads: send us your poem and we'll make it a record. Thousands of ordinary people paid. Session musicians set the lyrics in an afternoon, a few copies were pressed, and the record usually went nowhere except the customer's front room.

MSR 851 is one of these: "My Husband, Lover, Friend", sung by "Bobbi Blake" to words by Mary Bolton. It is a stranger's own words, paid into existence and then ignored. The American Song-Poem Music Archives keeps these discs listenable.

item.title: Haló: when towns went to war with songs
item.description:
Among the Anlo-Ewe of southeastern Ghana, haló was a war of insult songs between towns and factions: drums, dance, mime, costume and verses composed to wound. Fieldwork found it in about 88% of Anlo-Ewe towns. A local saying holds that being insulted in song is worse than a beating, because the song outlives you.

It was so powerful that Ghana banned it in its 1960 Criminal Code. We haven't yet found a recording, and the songs still name families. If you know of one, write to us.

item.title: Gnawa master meets a drummer who will not stop
item.description:
Maâlem Mahmoud Gania of Essaouira was the best-known Gnawa musician of his time. On a pair of Voix de Casablanca cassettes (VDC 53 and VDC 51), his guimbri and the clattering qraqeb are joined by an anonymous trap drummer who rolls, crashes and punctuates without a break.

The Moroccan Tape Stash blog called it one of the wildest tapes in its collection. The j-card names only "The Gnawi Mahmoud Guinia". Nobody knows who the drummer was.

item.title: Glory to the soldiers who would not shoot
item.description:
In June 1907 winegrowers in the Languedoc rose up against ruin. Soldiers of the 17th infantry regiment, many of them local men, were sent in and refused to fire on their own people. The chansonnier Montéhus wrote "Gloire au 17e" in their honour, and it was sung for decades as a hymn of collective refusal.

The original pre-1926 disc is still being hunted; Montéhus's 1936 remake streams on Phonobase.

item.title: Forty grimy cassettes behind the halal counter
item.description:
Gary Sullivan's Bodega Pop collects music ripped from cassettes and CDs found in immigrant-run corner shops. On one visit to a halal butcher's in Astoria he came away with some forty grime-encrusted tapes from Algeria, Egypt, Iraq, Lebanon, Morocco, Saudi Arabia, Syria, Turkey and the Emirates.

Most are commercial tapes nobody outside a diaspora shop would ever see. Some are wedding bands with no names on the j-card, and those are the ones we want.

item.title: Fifty copies and twenty years
item.description:
Yaw Atta-Owusu, as Ata Kak, recorded Obaa Sima in Toronto: Ghanaian highlife sped into home-made rap and drum machines. He pressed about fifty cassettes, sold a few in Ghana, and moved on with his life.

In 2002 a student found one of the tapes in a Ghanaian market stall. It took Awesome Tapes From Africa years to track him down. The 2015 reissue made a record nobody had wanted into one people won't stop playing.

item.title: Banned twice, once for a train
item.description:
Pērkons ("Thunder") were banned by the Soviet authorities in 1983. They carried on under an absurd cover name, the Ensemble of the Soviet Latvia Collective Farm.

On 6 July 1985 they played the open-air stage at Ogre. On the train home some teenage fans wrecked two carriages. The band wasn't on the train, but they were banned again anyway, and the fans got show trials, which Juris Podnieks filmed for Is It Easy to Be Young?. Their early home-studio recordings had already gone hand to hand on tape.

item.title: Answering a defeat from the year 451
item.description:
Ghevont Alishan's 1850 poem "Bam Porotan" calls Armenians to remember Avarayr, the battle of 451 in which Vartan Mamikonian fell defending the faith. That defeat has been commemorated for fifteen centuries.

In New York on 11 October 1916, with the Armenian Genocide still under way, Torcom Bézazian recorded it for Victor (69102, matrix B-18462). It is a diaspora singer keeping a very old account open, at the worst possible moment.

item.title: And Everything That Is Beautiful Is Beautiful
item.description:
In 1987 the painter Artūras "Šlipas" Šlipavičius and the record collector and dealer Artūras "Baras" Barysas started a band in the Vilnius underground. Many of their home tapes existed in a single copy. The name they chose was Ir Visa Tai Kas Yra Gražu Yra Gražu. The name they didn't choose translates as "Kill the close one, before the far one comes and kills you".

That rejected name could stand as the motto of this whole blog.

item.title: A son keeps his father's grudge
item.description:
In Wagner's Götterdämmerung, Hagen sits up all night guarding the hall while everyone else sleeps, turning over a revenge that was his father's before it was his. In 1922 the English bass Robert Radford recorded the scene in English for HMV, as "Hagen meditates revenge".

Grudges are often inherited. This is one of the earliest discs on which you can hear an inherited grievance being sung as a duty, slowly and in the dark.

item.title: A samba that mocked the police chief
item.description:
Samba grew up in Rio's Black neighbourhoods, around houses like Tia Ciata's, under constant police pressure. In January 1917 Casa Edison released "Pelo Telefone", credited to Donga and sung by Baiano on Odeon 121322. It was the hit of that year's carnival.

The popular version opens with the police chief phoning to say the fun can go ahead, a dig at police corruption hidden in a party song. A music the police harassed became Brazil's first samba hit, and its first line was a joke at the police's expense.

item.title: A prayer under occupation, and the tape that outlived the ban
item.description:
Lūcija Garūta wrote the cantata Dievs, Tava zeme deg! ("God, Thy Land Is Burning!") to words by Andrejs Eglītis while Latvia was being ground between two occupations. At its premiere on 15 March 1944 she played the organ herself, before a packed church and a crowd outside.

A tape of that premiere survives. One account says you can hear the war outside on it. The Soviet regime later suppressed the cantata. It came back by candlelight at the 1990 Song Festival, when the country was singing its way out.

item.title: A hymn recorded by the man who wrote the indictment
item.description:
In 1916 Sol Plaatje published Native Life in South Africa, a book-length charge sheet against the Natives' Land Act. On 16 October 1923, in London, he walked into Zonophone's studio and recorded six sides, with Sylvia Colenso at the piano.

One of them, without fanfare on the label, was Enoch Sontonga's "Nkosi Sikelel' iAfrika", the first recording of the hymn that became an anthem of liberation. It runs barely a minute. A prayer asking for Africa to be blessed, cut in the capital of the empire that had just shut the door on his delegation.

item.title: A guitar built from an oil can
item.description:
Wesseh "Weesay" Freeman lost his sight as a child and taught himself guitar to support his family. He built his own instruments from an oil can, a neck carved with a machete and strings made from bicycle cables. He played the streets of Monrovia for about four dollars a day, until a 2016 video of him playing went around the world.

He died in 2018. The guitar was made from things other people had thrown away, and that is part of why we wanted him here.

item.title: A corrido that names the man who sold the bandit
item.description:
Heraclio Bernal was a Sinaloa bandit-rebel betrayed for a reward in 1888. The corrido that followed made sure the betrayal was remembered as clearly as the man.

Trío Nava recorded "Heraclio Bernal" for Columbia in 1921. It is a ballad doing a newspaper's and a court's job at once: who did it, who paid, who sold whom. A transfer survives in UCLA's Frontera Collection of Mexican and Mexican-American recordings.

item.title: A congresswoman at the piano
item.description:
Malinda Jackson Parker was a former member of Liberia's House of Representatives who sat at the piano and half-sang, half-spoke her own songs: odes, praise songs, and a song about a mosquito. The Liberian Landmark Joy came out around 1971 and has been rediscovered abroad as "outsider music".

We would rather hear how she was heard at home: as a singular, self-made voice, and a woman's, in a style nobody else used.

item.title: 840 times
item.description:
Erik Satie left behind a single page of slow, unresolved music headed by a note about playing it 840 times in a row. He never published it and never played it.

On 9–10 September 1963 John Cage took the note at its word. At the Pocket Theatre in Manhattan a relay of pianists, among them John Cale, played it for 18 hours and 40 minutes. Ticket holders got a refund of a nickel for every 20 minutes they stayed.

item.title: 222 cassettes of Japanese weirdness
item.description:
In the 1980s a small circle around the composer K. Yoshimatsu and his associate Tadashi Kamada ran DD. Records. Over five years they released exactly 222 cassettes: ambient, abstract punk, musique concrète and fragile songs, each with typewritten notes and Xerox covers made from found material.

The original tapes are now collectors' dreams. A 2024 retrospective, Fossil Cocoon, finally made them easy to hear.
